title: AQA GCSE Biology · Infection and Response

items.stem: What is a pathogen?

options.text: A bacterium that causes an infectious disease
A poison that damages tissues and makes us ill
A microorganism that lives inside the body cells
A microorganism that causes infectious disease

items.why: Pathogens are microorganisms that cause infectious disease. They may be viruses, bacteria, protists or fungi, and may infect plants or animals.

items.stem: What kind of pathogen causes malaria?

options.text: A protist spread to humans by mosquitos
A bacterium spread to humans by mosquitos
A mosquito that bites and infects humans
A virus that reproduces in human cells

items.why: The pathogens that cause malaria are protists, and the malarial protist has a life cycle that includes the mosquito.

items.stem: Which of these is a non-specific defence system of the human body?

options.text: The nose produces antibodies to attack pathogens
The stomach produces acid that kills pathogens
Cilia in the trachea destroy trapped pathogens
White blood cells in the skin trap pathogens

items.why: The stomach is one of the non-specific defence systems of the human body: it produces hydrochloric acid that kills pathogens in swallowed food and mucus.

items.stem: What is introduced into the body during a vaccination?

options.text: Dead or inactive forms of a pathogen
Ready-made antibodies from donors
Live and active forms of a pathogen
An antibiotic that kills pathogens

items.why: Vaccination involves introducing small quantities of dead or inactive forms of a pathogen into the body to stimulate the white blood cells to produce antibodies.

items.stem: A pharmaceutical company has synthesised a possible new drug. Which describes the preclinical testing of that drug?

options.text: Testing on healthy volunteers, patients
Testing on cells, tissues and live animals
Testing on patients at the optimum dose
Testing on some patients given a placebo

items.why: Preclinical testing is done in a laboratory using cells, tissues and live animals, before the drug is given to any person.

items.stem: What happens in a double blind trial?

options.text: Some patients get a smaller dose
Healthy volunteers are in the trial
Some patients are given a placebo
Each patient gets the optimum dose

items.why: In double blind trials, some patients are given a placebo rather than the drug being tested.

items.stem: Which drug is correctly matched with the source it originally came from?

options.text: Aspirin is extracted from foxgloves
Penicillin is extracted from foxgloves
Digitalis is extracted from foxgloves
Digitalis is extracted from the willow

items.why: Traditionally drugs were extracted from plants and microorganisms, and the heart drug digitalis originates from foxgloves.

items.stem: Why must new medical drugs be tested and trialled before they are used?

options.text: To check they are safe and effective
To check they kill bacterial pathogens
To check they remove painful symptoms
To check patients cannot resist drugs

items.why: New medical drugs have to be tested and trialled before being used to check that they are safe and effective, which is why they are extensively tested for toxicity, efficacy and dose.

items.stem: How are most new drugs produced today?

options.text: Extracted from plants and microorganisms
Extracted from the willow and foxgloves
Collected from moulds growing in soil
Synthesised by pharmaceutical chemists

items.why: Most new drugs are synthesised by chemists in the pharmaceutical industry, although the starting point may still be a chemical extracted from a plant.

items.stem: Purple and black spots have appeared on the leaves of a rose bush in a garden. How is this disease most likely to reach the other rose bushes in the garden?

options.text: By insects moving between the plants
By direct contact between the leaves
By toxins spreading through the soil
By water or wind in the environment

items.why: Rose black spot is a fungal disease that is spread in the environment by water or wind, so it can cross the gap between plants that never touch.

items.stem: A health agency wants to reduce the number of malaria cases in a region. Which approach should it use?

options.text: Treating infected people with antibiotics
Stopping mosquitos breeding and using nets
Vaccinating whole populations against it
Avoiding direct contact with infected people

items.why: The spread of malaria is controlled by preventing the vectors, mosquitos, from breeding and by using mosquito nets to avoid being bitten.

items.stem: How is the spread of salmonella food poisoning controlled in the UK?

options.text: People are vaccinated against salmonella
Poultry are vaccinated against salmonella
Poultry are treated with strong antibiotics
People are given painkillers to cure it

items.why: Salmonella food poisoning is spread by bacteria ingested in food, and in the UK poultry are vaccinated against salmonella to control the spread.

items.stem: Bacteria in the blood are releasing toxins. Which action of the white blood cells deals with those toxins?

options.text: The production of antibodies
The engulfing of the bacteria
The production of antitoxins
The production of stomach acid

items.why: White blood cells help to defend against pathogens by antitoxin production, and antitoxins counteract the toxins that bacteria produce.

items.stem: A pathogen gets past the body's non-specific defences and enters the body for the first time. What does the immune system do?

options.text: It produces toxins to kill the pathogen
It tries to destroy the invading pathogen
It develops resistance to the pathogen
It waits for a vaccination to be given

items.why: If a pathogen enters the body the immune system tries to destroy the pathogen, using phagocytosis, antibody production and antitoxin production.

items.stem: A large proportion of the population in a town is vaccinated against measles. What is the effect on the people in that town who are not vaccinated?

options.text: They are equally likely to catch measles
They are made immune to measles as well
They are less likely to catch measles
They must be given antibiotics instead

items.why: The spread of pathogens can be reduced by immunising a large proportion of the population, so an unvaccinated person is less likely to meet the measles virus.

items.stem: A patient has a viral infection and a painful sore throat. Which treatment is appropriate, and why?

options.text: Antibiotics, which kill the pathogen
Painkillers, which destroy the virus
Painkillers, which treat the symptoms
Antitoxins, which kill the pathogen

items.why: Painkillers and other medicines are used to treat the symptoms of disease but do not kill pathogens, so they are the appropriate treatment for the pain of a viral infection.

items.stem: Why is it difficult to develop drugs that kill viruses?

options.text: Viruses live in cells, so tissues are damaged
Viruses reproduce outside the body's cells
Viruses make toxins that destroy the drugs
Viruses are easily destroyed by antibiotics

items.why: Viruses live and reproduce inside cells, so it is difficult to develop drugs that kill viruses without also damaging the body's tissues.

items.stem: The use of antibiotics greatly reduced deaths from infectious bacterial diseases, but some bacterial infections are now much harder to treat. Why?

options.text: Patients have grown resistant to antibiotics
Antibiotics have started to kill viruses too
Bacteria now reproduce inside human cells
Resistant strains of bacteria have emerged

items.why: The emergence of strains resistant to antibiotics is of great concern, because those strains are not killed by the antibiotic that once cured the disease.

items.stem: Which statement about monoclonal antibodies is correct?

options.text: They create more side effects than expected.
They bind to several different protein antigens.
They create fewer side effects than expected.
They kill cancer cells with no substance bound.

items.why: Correct. Monoclonal antibodies create more side effects than expected, and they are not yet as widely used as everyone hoped when they were first developed.

items.stem: Mouse lymphocytes are stimulated to make a particular antibody. They are then combined with a particular kind of tumour cell. What does the tumour cell allow the hybridoma cell to do?

options.text: Make the antibody that is later collected.
Make a different antibody as it divides.
Divide to produce many identical cells.
Kill the cells the antibody binds to.

items.why: Correct. The hybridoma cell can both divide and make the antibody, and single hybridoma cells are cloned to produce many identical cells that all produce the same antibody.

items.stem: A patient with cancer is given a monoclonal antibody that has been bound to a toxic drug. The antibody binds to an antigen found on the patient's cancer cells. How does this treatment work?

options.text: It carries the toxic drug to every body cell.
It stops the toxic drug causing side effects.
It destroys the cancer cells as it binds to them.
It delivers the toxic drug to the cancer cells.

items.why: Correct. For cancer the monoclonal antibody can be bound to a toxic drug, and it delivers the substance to the cancer cells without harming other cells in the body.

items.stem: A monoclonal antibody is collected from a clone of hybridoma cells and used to measure the level of one hormone in blood. Why does it bind only to that hormone?

options.text: It is made by a mixture of many different cells.
It is specific to one binding site on one antigen.
It is made by one particular kind of tumour cell.
It is able to bind any antigen in the sample.

items.why: Correct. Monoclonal antibodies are specific to one binding site on one protein antigen and so are able to target a specific chemical in the body.

items.stem: Which of these plant problems is caused by a fungal pathogen?

options.text: Black spot, giving dark marks on rose leaves
Aphid infestation, giving reduced plant growth
Chlorosis, giving yellow patches on leaves
Tobacco mosaic virus, giving a mosaic pattern

items.why: Black spot is the named fungal disease of plants: purple or black spots develop on the leaves, which often turn yellow and drop early.

items.stem: Which of these is a physical defence response that resists invasion of microorganisms?

options.text: Poisons which are made in the leaves
Hairs which grow on the leaf surfaces
Leaves which curl when they are touched
Layers of dead cells around the stems

items.why: Layers of dead cells around stems (bark on trees), which fall off, are a physical defence response that resists invasion of microorganisms.

items.stem: A plant has grown to the normal height for its age, but its leaves have turned yellow. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: A lack of nitrate ions, needed to make chlorophyll
A lack of magnesium ions, needed to make chlorophyll
An infection by black spot, a fungal plant disease
An attack by aphids, which are plant microorganisms

items.why: Magnesium ions are needed to make chlorophyll, so a magnesium deficiency causes chlorosis, in which the leaves turn yellow while height can stay normal.

items.stem: A rose plant has sharp thorns on its stems. Which type of plant defence is this?

options.text: A physical defence that resists microorganisms
A chemical defence that kills invading bacteria
A sign of infection by a fungal plant pathogen
A mechanical adaptation that deters animals

items.why: Thorns and hairs deter animals, so they are listed as mechanical adaptations rather than as physical or chemical defence responses.

items.stem: A grower sees stunted growth and discoloured leaves on a crop, and a gardening website does not settle what is wrong. What should be done next to identify the cause?

options.text: Add nitrate fertiliser to the soil to restore leaf colour
Spray the whole crop with a fungicide to kill black spot
Take the plant to a laboratory to identify the pathogen
Look for a mosaic pattern to confirm a fungal disease

items.why: Identification can be made by taking infected plants to a laboratory to identify the pathogen, which is the step to take when a gardening manual or website is not enough.
